question: In a haemodynamically unstable pelvic fracture patient who fails to respond to resuscitation and pelvic binder application, angioembolisation (IR) should be attempted as the first definitive haemorrhage-control procedure before any surgical intervention.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is FALSE. Angioembolisation is excellent for arterial haemorrhage but is not the first-line for the truly unstable patient because of time-to-suite delays. Immediate pre-peritoneal packing (PPP) or REBOA is preferred in haemodynamic non-responders. Review the ATLS damage-control sequence for pelvic fracture haemorrhage.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is FALSE. In the truly unstable patient (BP < 90 mmHg despite initial resuscitation), the time delay required for IR suite setup is often not acceptable. Current ATLS-aligned protocols favour immediate pre-peritoneal packing (PPP) or REBOA as the first surgical step in haemodynamic instability, with angioembolisation reserved for patients who stabilise briefly (transient responders) or after damage-control packing. IR is more effective for arterial bleeders, which account for only ~20% of pelvic haemorrhage.
